subject: Physics
title: Heat and Thermodynamics
learningOutcomes: State that regions at equal temperature are in thermal equilibrium.
Relate a rise in temperature of an object to an increase in its internal energy.
Apply the equation of state PV = nRT for an ideal gas.
State that the Boltzmann constant is given by k = R/N_A.
Describe the basic assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases.
Use W = PΔV for the work done when the volume of a gas changes at constant pressure.
Describe the difference between the work done by a gas and the work done on a gas.
Define and use the first law of thermodynamics, Q = ΔU + W.
Explain qualitatively, in terms of particles, the relationship between the pressure, temperature and volume of a gas.
Use the equation and the graph of the relationship between pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature.
Justify how the first law of thermodynamics expresses the conservation of energy.
Relate a rise in temperature of a body to an increase in its internal energy.
State the working principle of a heat engine.
Describe the concept of reversible and irreversible processes.
State and explain the second law of thermodynamics.
State the working principle of Carnot's engine.
Describe a refrigerator as a heat engine operating in reverse as that of an ideal heat engine.
Explain that an increase in temperature increases the disorder of the system.
Explain that an increase in entropy means degradation of energy.
Explain that energy is degraded during all natural processes.
Identify that a system tends to become less orderly over time.
Explain that entropy S is a thermodynamic quantity related to the degree of disorder of the particles in a system.
State that the Carnot cycle sets a limit for the efficiency of a heat engine at the temperatures of its reservoirs: efficiency = 1 − T_cold/T_hot.

sections.heading: Temperature, Heat and Thermal Equilibrium
sections.body: Temperature is the degree of hotness or coldness of a body and measures the average kinetic energy of its molecules; its SI unit is the kelvin (K). Heat is the energy associated with the kinetic energies of all the molecules in a substance; its unit is the joule (J). Two systems are in thermal equilibrium when they are at the same temperature, and heat flows from the body at higher temperature to the one at lower temperature until the temperatures become equal. Always convert °C to kelvin with T = t + 273 before using any gas law.

sections.heading: System, Surroundings and Boundary
sections.body: The matter or region of space under study is the system; everything outside it is the surroundings, and the surface separating them is the boundary. All energy exchange by heat or work takes place through the boundary. An open system exchanges both heat and mass (an open beaker), a closed system exchanges heat but not mass (a sealed container), and an isolated system exchanges neither (a thermos flask of hot water).

sections.heading: Internal Energy
sections.body: The internal energy of a substance is the sum of all the kinetic and potential energies of its molecules. In an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so the internal energy is only the translational kinetic energy of the molecules, ⟨½mv²⟩ = (3/2)kT, and is directly proportional to the absolute temperature. Internal energy is a function of state: ΔU = U₂ − U₁ depends only on the initial and final states, not on the path. ΔU is positive when T rises, negative when T falls and zero when T stays constant. It can be raised by heating a body or by doing work on it.

sections.heading: Ideal Gas Equation and Boltzmann Constant
sections.body: An ideal gas has particles of negligible volume, no attractive or repulsive forces and perfectly elastic collisions. Its equation of state is PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹. Writing n = N/N_A gives PV = NkT where the Boltzmann constant k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹. The density of an ideal gas is ρ = PM/RT. A real gas behaves like an ideal gas at low pressure and high temperature, when the density is low and intermolecular forces are negligible.

sections.heading: Kinetic Theory of Gases
sections.body: The kinetic theory, developed by Maxwell, Clausius and others, relates macroscopic properties such as pressure and temperature to molecular motion. Its assumptions: a gas contains a very large number of molecules; the molecules are much smaller than the distance between them; they move randomly and change direction after every collision, and the collisions with each other and with the walls are perfectly elastic; they exert no forces on each other except during a collision. Pressure comes from molecules striking the walls, so heating a gas at constant volume makes the molecules hit harder and more often and raises P.

sections.heading: Work Done by a Gas
sections.body: A gas at pressure P pushing a piston of area A exerts a force F = PA. When the piston moves a small distance Δy the work is W = PAΔy = PΔV, and the work done by the gas at constant pressure is W = PΔV. On a P–V graph the work equals the area under the curve. When the gas expands (ΔV > 0) the work done by the gas is positive; when it is compressed (ΔV < 0) the work done by the gas is negative and work is done on the gas; if the volume is constant the work is zero.

sections.heading: The Gas Laws
sections.body: For a fixed amount of gas with temperature in kelvin: Boyle's law (constant T) PV = constant, a hyperbola on a P–V graph; Charles's law (constant P) V/T = constant, a straight line on a V–T graph that meets −273 °C at zero volume; Gay-Lussac's or Amontons's law (constant V) P/T = constant, a straight line through the origin on a P–T graph. All three follow from PV = nRT.

sections.heading: First Law of Thermodynamics
sections.body: When heat Q is added to a system it raises the internal energy by ΔU and the system does work W on its surroundings: Q = ΔU + W. This is the law of conservation of energy applied to heat and work. Q is positive when heat is added and negative when it is removed; W is positive when the system does work and negative when work is done on it. Examples are melting ice, sweating, pumping a tyre and human metabolism.

sections.heading: Isothermal and Adiabatic Processes
sections.body: In an isothermal process the temperature is constant, so for an ideal gas ΔU = 0 and Q = W; PV = constant, the curve is an isotherm, and the process must be slow so heat can flow. In an adiabatic process no heat is transferred, so Q = 0 and W = −ΔU; the process is rapid, the curve (adiabat) is steeper than the isotherm, an expanding gas cools and a compressed gas warms.

sections.heading: Isochoric and Isobaric Processes
sections.body: In an isochoric process the volume is constant, so W = 0 and Q = ΔU; the P–V graph is a vertical line (isochor), as in a pressure cooker. In an isobaric process the pressure is constant, so Q = ΔU + PΔV; the P–V graph is a horizontal line (isobar) and the area under it is the work, as when water boils in an open pan.

sections.heading: Heat Engine
sections.body: A heat engine converts heat into mechanical work. It needs a hot reservoir (source, T₁, supplies Q₁), a cold reservoir (sink, T₂, absorbs Q₂) and a working substance, usually a gas, and it operates in cycles. The work per cycle is W = Q₁ − Q₂ and the efficiency is η = W/Q₁ = 1 − Q₂/Q₁. The working principle rests on the second law. A four-stroke petrol engine has intake, compression, power and exhaust strokes and an efficiency of only about 25% to 30%.

sections.heading: Reversible, Irreversible and Cyclic Processes
sections.body: A reversible process can be retraced in the reverse order without changing the surroundings; no real process is exactly reversible, but slow ones can be treated as such. Friction, decay, and heat flow by conduction, convection or radiation are irreversible. A cyclic process brings the system back to its initial state, so the net change in internal energy over a cycle is zero.

sections.heading: Second Law of Thermodynamics
sections.body: The first law does not tell the direction of natural processes; the second law does. Kelvin's statement: no heat engine can convert heat taken from a single reservoir entirely into work. Clausius's statement: heat cannot flow from a cold body to a hot body without the expenditure of work. In terms of entropy, a natural process proceeds in the direction in which the entropy of the system plus the environment increases.

sections.heading: Carnot's Engine
sections.body: The Carnot engine is a theoretical engine working on a reversible cycle of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes: isothermal expansion at T₁ (heat Q₁ absorbed), adiabatic expansion (T₁ to T₂), isothermal compression at T₂ (heat Q₂ rejected) and adiabatic compression (T₂ to T₁). ΔU = 0 over the cycle, so W = Q₁ − Q₂ equals the area enclosed. Its efficiency η = 1 − T₂/T₁ depends only on the reservoir temperatures and never reaches 100%. Carnot's theorem: no engine between the same two temperatures is more efficient.

sections.heading: Refrigerator and Heat Pump
sections.body: A refrigerator is a heat engine run in reverse: the compressor does work W on the refrigerant, which takes heat Q₂ from the cold inside and rejects Q₁ = Q₂ + W to the room. Work is needed because heat does not flow from cold to hot by itself. The coefficient of performance for cooling is CP = Q₂/W = T₂/(T₁ − T₂) for an ideal refrigerator; used to heat a space the device is a heat pump with CP = T₁/(T₁ − T₂).

sections.heading: Entropy
sections.body: Entropy S is a state variable that measures the degree of disorder of the particles and the unavailability of thermal energy for work. For a reversible process ΔS = ΔQ/T (unit J K⁻¹), positive when heat is added and negative when heat is removed. Ice melting, boiling and sublimation increase entropy; freezing and condensation decrease it. Heat flowing from T₁ to T₂ < T₁ gives ΔS = Q/T₂ − Q/T₁ > 0. Entropy stays constant in reversible processes and increases in irreversible ones; an increase in entropy means degradation of energy, and entropy gives time its arrow.

definitions.definition: The degree of hotness or coldness of a body; a measure of the average kinetic energy of its molecules (unit: kelvin).
The form of energy associated with the kinetic energies of all the molecules in a substance (unit: joule).
The branch of physics that studies the transformation of heat into other forms of energy.
The energy possessed by a system due to the movement of its particles (book summary).
The state of two systems at the same temperature, with no net heat flow between them.
The matter or region of space that is being studied.
Everything outside the system.
A system in which neither heat nor mass crosses the boundary.
The sum of all the kinetic and potential energies of the molecules of a substance.
The gas constant per molecule, k = R/N_A = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J K⁻¹.
A gas whose particles have negligible volume, exert no forces on each other and collide perfectly elastically.
The volume of a given amount of gas at constant temperature is inversely proportional to its pressure: PV = constant.
The volume of a given amount of gas at constant pressure is directly proportional to its absolute temperature: V/T = constant.
The pressure of a given amount of gas at constant volume is directly proportional to its absolute temperature: P/T = constant.
Heat added to a system increases its internal energy and does work on the surroundings: Q = ΔU + W.
A process that takes place at constant temperature, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W for an ideal gas.
A process in which no heat is transferred between the system and its surroundings, so Q = 0 and W = −ΔU.
A process at constant volume, so W = 0 and Q = ΔU.
A process at constant pressure, so Q = ΔU + PΔV.
A device that converts heat into mechanical work using a hot reservoir, a cold reservoir and a working substance.
A process that can be retraced in exactly the reverse order without any change in the surroundings.
No heat engine can convert heat taken from a single reservoir entirely into work.
Heat cannot flow from a cold body to a hot body without the expenditure of work.
η = 1 − T₂/T₁, the maximum efficiency of an engine working between a source at T₁ and a sink at T₂ (in kelvin).
For a refrigerator, the heat removed from the cold region divided by the work done: CP = Q₂/W = T₂/(T₁ − T₂).
A thermodynamic state variable measuring the disorder of the particles of a system; ΔS = ΔQ/T.

examTips: Convert °C to kelvin (T = t + 273) before using any gas law, Carnot efficiency or coefficient of performance. Using °C is the most common error in this unit.
Write the first law as Q = ΔU + W with W the work done BY the gas: expansion gives W > 0, compression gives W < 0, and heat removed gives Q < 0.
Memorise the four processes with one picture each: isothermal Q = W, adiabatic W = −ΔU, isochoric Q = ΔU, isobaric Q = ΔU + PΔV. Each is the first law with one term removed or kept.
In a complete cycle ΔU = 0, so the net work is W = Q₁ − Q₂; this is the area enclosed by the loop on the P–V diagram.
For a Carnot engine use η = 1 − T₂/T₁ with T₁ the hotter reservoir. To raise the efficiency, raise T₁ (the sink is usually the atmosphere); 100% is impossible.
For an ideal refrigerator CP (cooling) = T₂/(T₁ − T₂) and CP (heating) = T₁/(T₁ − T₂); the heat delivered to the room is Q₁ = Q₂ + W.

Entropy increases when heat is added, when a solid melts or sublimes, and in every irreversible process; it decreases when heat is removed, in freezing and in condensation. Entropy of the universe never decreases.
In long answers state the law, write the formula with symbols named, then give one example; examiners reward the sign conventions and units.
A common mistake: calling an isothermal process the same as an adiabatic one. Isothermal keeps T constant (heat flows), adiabatic keeps Q = 0 (the temperature changes).

practiceQuestions.prompt: Two systems are in thermal equilibrium with each other when they have the same:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Equal temperature is the only condition for thermal equilibrium; there is no net heat flow.

practiceQuestions.prompt: For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process, the change in internal energy is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: The temperature is constant and U of an ideal gas depends only on T, so ΔU = 0 and Q = W.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A gas in a rigid vessel is heated. Its pressure rises in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. This is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: At constant volume P/T is constant: Gay-Lussac's (Amontons's) law.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A gas occupies 6 L at 2 atm. It is compressed isothermally to 3 atm. Its new volume is:
practiceQuestions.explanation: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂, so V₂ = (2 × 6)/3 = 4 L.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A gas expands at a constant pressure of 2 × 10⁵ Pa from 0.01 m³ to 0.04 m³. The work done by the gas is:
A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work. The change in its internal energy is:
A Carnot engine works between 600 K and 300 K. Its efficiency is:
A refrigerator needs a compressor and electric power because:

options: Heat does not flow from cold to hot without work
Cold flows out of the box
Heat is created inside the box
The gas has no internal energy

practiceQuestions.explanation: By Clausius's statement work must be done to move heat from a cold region to a hot one.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In an adiabatic process no heat is transferred between the system and its surroundings.
A heat engine can convert all the heat it takes from a single hot reservoir into work.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. By Kelvin's statement some heat Q₂ must be rejected to a cold reservoir, so W = Q₁ − Q₂ < Q₁.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The entropy of water increases when ice melts.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Heat is absorbed (ΔS = ΔQ/T > 0) and the ordered crystal becomes a randomly moving liquid.

practiceQuestions.prompt: In the gas laws the temperature may be used in degrees Celsius without any change.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The proportionalities V ∝ T and P ∝ T hold only for the absolute (kelvin) scale: T = t + 273.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The Boltzmann constant is k = R divided by the ______ number.
In an isochoric process the work done by the gas is ______.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The volume does not change, so W = PΔV = 0 and Q = ΔU.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The unit of entropy is joule per ______.
practiceQuestions.explanation: ΔS = ΔQ/T, so the unit is J K⁻¹.

sequencingActivity.prompt: Arrange the four steps of the Carnot cycle in the correct order, starting with isothermal expansion.

items: Adiabatic compression (temperature rises from T₂ to T₁)
Isothermal expansion at T₁ (heat Q₁ absorbed)
Isothermal compression at T₂ (heat Q₂ rejected)
Adiabatic expansion (temperature falls from T₁ to T₂)
correctOrder: Isothermal expansion at T₁ (heat Q₁ absorbed)
Adiabatic expansion (temperature falls from T₁ to T₂)
Isothermal compression at T₂ (heat Q₂ rejected)
Adiabatic compression (temperature rises from T₂ to T₁)

sequencingActivity.explanation: Heat is exchanged only in the isothermal steps (Q₁ in at T₁, Q₂ out at T₂); the adiabatic steps move the gas between the two temperatures with no heat flow.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A Carnot engine takes 1200 J per cycle from a source at 600 K and rejects heat to a sink at 300 K. If the sink is cooled to 200 K (source and Q₁ unchanged), the extra work per cycle is:
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: At 300 K: η = 0.50 and W = 600 J. At 200 K: η = 1 − 200/600 = 2/3 and W = 800 J. The extra work is 800 − 600 = 200 J.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: An ideal refrigerator keeps its inside at 270 K in a room at 300 K. For every 500 J of work done by the compressor, the heat removed from the inside is:
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: CP = T₂/(T₁ − T₂) = 270/30 = 9, so Q₂ = 9 × 500 = 4500 J (and the room receives 5000 J).

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: A gas absorbs 6 kJ of heat while expanding from 0.01 m³ to 0.03 m³ at a constant pressure of 2 × 10⁵ Pa. The change in its internal energy is:
1200 J of heat flows by conduction from a body at 600 K to a body at 300 K. The net change in entropy of the two bodies is:
bossBattleQuestions.explanation: ΔS = Q/T₂ − Q/T₁ = 1200/300 − 1200/600 = 4 − 2 = +2 J K⁻¹: positive, as for every irreversible process.

bossBattleQuestions.prompt: 4 atm of ideal gas at 3 L expands slowly at constant temperature to 12 L. Which statement is correct?

options: The final pressure is 1 atm and the heat absorbed equals the work done
The final pressure is 1 atm and the internal energy rises
The final pressure is 16 atm and ΔU = 0
The final pressure is 1 atm and no heat is absorbed

bossBattleQuestions.explanation: Boyle's law: P₂ = (4 × 3)/12 = 1 atm. The process is isothermal, so ΔU = 0 and all the heat absorbed becomes work, Q = W.
